title: How to Keep Grades Up While Buried in Coursework
summary: Learn how to keep grades up while buried in coursework during the IB DP2 fall term with a practical September-November plan for every subject.
body_markdown:
The **IB DP2 fall term** creates a difficult balancing problem. Internal assessments, the Extended Essay, TOK, university applications, tests, and ordinary homework compete for limited time. To keep grades up while buried in coursework, use two parallel systems: protected coursework blocks for major submissions and short exam-practice sessions that prevent subject knowledge from fading.


The goal from September to November is not to study every subject equally each day. It is to finish urgent coursework without allowing any subject to disappear from your schedule for weeks.


### Why grades often fall during the IB DP2 fall term


Coursework deadlines are visible and immediate. A test three weeks away feels less urgent than an IA draft due tomorrow, so revision is repeatedly postponed. By November, students may have completed substantial coursework but forgotten earlier content or lost fluency with exam questions.


Vague tasks also waste time. Instructions such as “work on Biology IA” or “revise History” encourage long sessions with unclear outcomes. Replace them with measurable deliverables, such as “interpret the final graph” or “plan one essay using three examples.”


The IB communicates official submission dates to schools, while schools normally set earlier internal deadlines for students. The IB pages on[Extended Essay submission deadlines](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/extended-essay/submission-deadline/) and[TOK submission deadlines](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/theory-of-knowledge/upload-deadline/) direct students to their schools for local dates. Your coordinator’s calendar is therefore the deadline you must follow.


### Use a two-track system to keep grades up while buried


Separate your work into a **coursework track** and a **subject-maintenance track** . Both should appear in your weekly plan, although their relative weight can change.


Track Purpose Typical tasks Weekly protection


Coursework Move major submissions toward completion Analyse IA data, draft an EE section, check citations Substantial blocks based on the nearest deadline


Subject maintenance Preserve knowledge and exam technique Retrieval, question sets, essay plans, error correction At least one meaningful contact with every subject


A coursework-heavy week might allocate most independent study time to an IA and EE. That still does not justify abandoning Mathematics, a language, or an essay subject. A focused **20-30 minute** session can preserve retrieval and expose confusion before it becomes a large gap.


RevisionDojo’s[balanced IB study schedule](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-create-a-balanced-ib-study-schedule) provides a broader model for distributing focused work, recall, and rest.


### Build your September-November plan


### September: map the workload


Place every confirmed school deadline, test, oral, application task, and fixed commitment in one calendar. Work backward from each coursework deadline, adding milestones for research, data collection, analysis, drafting, feedback, revision, referencing, and proofreading.


Every planned session needs a deliverable. Instead of “finish EE,” write “revise the argument in section two using three cited sources.” This makes progress visible and helps you restart efficiently.


Complete a short diagnostic check in every subject using a recent test, exam-style questions, or blank-page recall. Classify topics as **secure** , **developing** , or **weak** . RevisionDojo’s[IB resources hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib) includes Study Notes, Flashcards, and topic-based practice for this process.


### October: protect minimum viable revision


October is often when several drafts overlap. Establish a minimum revision floor that remains in place during difficult weeks:


- **10-15 minutes** of recall on most days
- Two or three short exam-question sets across priority subjects
- One essay plan or timed paragraph for a writing-based subject
- One weekly review of mistakes and teacher feedback
- At least one contact with every subject


This is academic maintenance rather than full exam preparation. Use active methods: reconstruct a process without notes, explain a concept aloud, answer questions, or plan a response under a short time limit. The[IB coursework study guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/comprehensive-guide-to-ib-coursework-study-tips) explains how to combine drafting with exam practice.


### November: begin cumulative revision


By November, reconnect current lessons with DP1 material. Choose one weak area in each subject, retrieve what you know, review a targeted explanation, apply the knowledge, and correct your response.


You do not necessarily need full papers yet. Timed sections, structured questions, and essay outlines fit more easily around coursework and provide clearer diagnostic information. The[IB exam-preparation timeline](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-long-before-the-ib-exam-should-i-start-preparing-for-it-a-smart-student-s-timeline-for-success) shows how this practice can develop into mock preparation later in DP2.


### Prioritize by consequence, urgency, and weakness


Rank work using three questions:


1. **Consequence:** How much does the task affect a subject, core requirement, or school decision?
2. **Urgency:** When is the next genuine deadline or assessment?
3. **Weakness:** Where are you currently losing marks or lacking understanding?


A nearly complete IA due in two days will usually outrank general revision. However, a major Chemistry test tomorrow still deserves protected preparation. Reassess priorities weekly because the correct order changes.


Limit your weekly list to **three major outcomes** . Smaller tasks can remain underneath, but three central outcomes create a realistic definition of progress.


### Make each study block produce evidence


A productive session should leave visible evidence: a completed paragraph, corrected question set, improved graph, essay outline, source table, or list of error rules. Time spent is not reliable evidence of learning.


For subject revision, use this compact cycle:


1. Retrieve the idea without notes.
2. Check a concise explanation.
3. Apply it to an exam-style question.
4. Mark the response and diagnose lost marks.
5. Retest the weakness within several days.


For coursework, work criterion by criterion rather than repeatedly polishing the introduction. The RevisionDojo[Coursework Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader) provides rubric-aligned diagnostic feedback on IA, EE, and TOK drafts. It is not official IB marking, so verify suggestions, use teacher feedback, and preserve your own reasoning and authorship.


### Manage difficult weeks without abandoning the plan


When a week collapses, reduce task size rather than deleting entire subjects. A **minimum viable day** might include one 25-minute coursework block, ten minutes of retrieval, and one corrected exam question.


If a deadline is genuinely at risk, contact the teacher or coordinator early. Explain what is complete, what remains, and what support you need. Do not assume an extension is available.


Protect sleep as an academic resource. Late-night work often produces weak analysis, careless referencing, and poor recall. Set a stopping time and record the exact next action so the following session begins promptly.


### Common mistakes to avoid


- **Giving coursework every available hour:** Subject knowledge and test performance deteriorate.
- **Treating all subjects equally:** Tests, weaknesses, and HL demands should affect allocation.
- **Polishing too early:** Complete the argument, evidence, and analysis before formatting.
- **Using passive revision:** Rereading does not prove you can retrieve or apply knowledge.
- **Ignoring feedback:** Convert each important comment into a specific action.
- **Copying AI-generated material:** This threatens academic integrity and prevents genuine learning.
- **Planning without recovery:** A schedule dependent on perfect concentration is unsustainable.


### Conclusion


To keep grades up while buried in coursework, manage coursework and subject maintenance as separate but connected tracks. Follow school deadlines, define concrete weekly outputs, preserve short active-recall sessions, and begin cumulative revision in November.
